extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, publishers, and editorial staff (health research journals)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for journals on adopting and integrating reporting guidelines into editorial workflows to improve transparency, reproducibility, and usability of health research manuscripts. Covers purpose, common objections, implementation routes, and resources for different study types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of reporting guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporting guidelines are here to make all of our lives easier – author, reader, peer reviewer, journal, and systematic reviewer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A weight of evidence has found many health research articles are not fit for purpose: they lack information needed to understand, evaluate, replicate, or include in systematic reviews. Reporting guidelines define the minimum set of information each group needs for a particular study type. If authors use reporting guidelines when writing, manuscripts can be understood, replicated, and used in clinical decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use guidelines during writing, not just at submission
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporting guidelines should be used while writing an article, not as a box-checking exercise at the submission stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Initial compliance may be poor when first implemented. The toolkit includes a template letter requesting resubmission once an article has been made compliant and explanation materials. Educating authors should lead them to integrate guidelines into their writing process and eventually into research design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require checklist as a completeness review
rubrics_metrics.description: Some journals require authors to submit a checklist indicating the page number on which each guideline information item has been addressed; this helps authors to report every necessary item, acting as a 'completeness review'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is not simply an administrative hurdle — it supports completeness and transparency. The toolkit provides editable checklists and template instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endorsement improves reporting quality
rubrics_metrics.description: We see a significant increase in reporting quality when a journal endorses a reporting guideline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence indicates endorsement by a journal is associated with better reporting. The site links to evidence and tools demonstrating the positive impact of using reporting guidelines and the impact of not using them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer and editorial review alone are insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Existing peer and editorial review are not enough to ensure complete reporting; every specialty and study type checked suffers from poor reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporting guidelines are a helpful tool for peer reviewers, allowing systematic checks that ensure essential information is present rather than relying on ad hoc reviewer detection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implementation routes: 'endorse' versus 'require checklist'
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals can implement guidelines via a simple 'endorse' route (change Instructions to Authors and link to guidelines) or a 'require checklist' route (require checklist submission and compliance checks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'endorse' route is low-effort and places no requirement on authors; the 'require checklist' route can include training editorial staff to check compliance during triage, asking a first reviewer to check compliance before recruiting others, and returning manuscripts that fail compliance until corrected. The toolkit supplies workflows, template letters, reviewer instructions, and editable checklists to support both routes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial triage and staff checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Some journals train editorial administrative staff to check guideline compliance on submission as part of submission triage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a manuscript fails compliance at triage, peer review can be halted and the article returned for resubmission after correction. Triage checks can be performed in minutes, reducing burden on peer reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implementing guidelines does not reduce submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals that have used either the 'require' or 'endorse' routes have found no significant change in their submission rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If concerned about losing submissions, journals can start with the 'endorse' route which places no requirements on authors. Some specialties have achieved critical mass where authors expect guideline use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implementing guidelines speeds up publication of well-reported articles
rubrics_metrics.description: Implementing reporting guidelines speeds up publication of well-reported articles and speeds up rejection of poorly reported articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benefits include: authors have a clear template when writing; editors can quickly triage and return poorly reported manuscripts in minutes rather than sending them for lengthy peer review; peer reviewers spend less time on manuscripts that need substantial rewriting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using guidelines does not necessarily delay peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer reviewers can use reporting guidelines as a tool to quickly triage and send back poorly reported manuscripts, reducing the time they spend reviewing an article that needs substantial rewriting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fully reported studies make it easier to judge methodological quality because crucial information is presented; reviewers do not need to hunt for details or guess what was done.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidelines do not make articles formulaic or stifle creativity
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporting guidelines give a minimum set of information that must be included for transparency, reproducibility, and usability; they do not prescribe the language authors should use or how to write introduction, discussion, or interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidelines focus mainly on methods and results. A creatively written article that cannot be understood or used is not a scientific article; guidelines ensure scientific usefulness without dictating prose style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Low-cost implementation options exist
rubrics_metrics.description: My journal can’t afford to implement reporting guidelines — rebuttal: the toolkit includes tools and a workflow for the simple 'endorse' route that only requires a change to 'Instructions to Authors' and links for authors to get reporting guidelines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'endorse' route is a low-cost starting point; the toolkit provides resources to reduce implementation burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting quality is a shared responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Good reporting isn’t a journal’s responsibility — counterpoint: good reporting is everyone’s responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors, reviewers, editors, and publishers all have roles in ensuring manuscripts include the minimum information necessary for use and reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author burden vs methodological rigor
rubrics_metrics.description: Implementing guidelines is sometimes seen as onerous for authors, but reporting guidelines offer authors a clear template which may initially lengthen writing if items were not previously considered; this often reveals methodological flaws that should be addressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longer writing time for poorly planned items is preferable to sending flawed work through peer review and wasting reviewers' time; guidelines can therefore save overall effort in the research/publication lifecycle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use guidelines at research design phase
rubrics_metrics.description: As authors become educated about reporting guidelines, they will integrate their use in their writing process and, eventually, use them at the research design phase, to ensure every item requested by a guideline has been considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proactive use during design improves study conduct and subsequent reporting completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match study type to the appropriate reporting guideline (resource list)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporting guidelines exist for main study types (randomised trials, observational studies, systematic reviews, protocols, diagnostic studies, case reports, clinical practice guidelines, qualitative research, animal pre-clinical studies, quality improvement, economic evaluations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples listed: Randomised trials — CONSORT (+extensions); Observational studies — STROBE (+extensions); Systematic reviews — PRISMA (+extensions); Study protocols — SPIRIT/PRISMA-P; Diagnostic/prognostic — STARD/TRIPOD; Case reports — CARE; Clinical practice guidelines — AGREE/RIGHT; Qualitative — SRQR/COREQ; Animal pre-clinical — ARRIVE; Quality improvement — SQUIRE (+extensions); Economic evaluations — CHEERS (+extensions). Use the guideline appropriate to the study type or specific methods/outcomes.
